sections.title: Thirty cents an hour and the size of the universe
sections.intro_md:
In 1908 a woman at Harvard College Observatory sat at a wooden frame with a glass photographic plate lit from below and a magnifier in her hand. Her job was to compare thousands of black dots, one plate against another, and note which stars had changed brightness. She was paid 30 cents an hour. She was going deaf.

Henrietta Swan Leavitt noticed something in a smudge of the southern sky called the Small Magellanic Cloud. Its blinking stars were all roughly the same distance from Earth, so their differences in brightness were real. And the brighter ones blinked more slowly. In 1912 she published a graph of 25 of them. The line was so clean that a star's rhythm told you its true power. Compare that to how bright it looks, and you know how far away it is.

Within 13 years that graph had shown that the Milky Way is one galaxy among countless others. Within 20, it had shown the universe is expanding. Today it sits in the middle of a chain of methods that astronomers call the distance ladder, and that chain is now giving an answer that does not match the universe's baby picture. This is the story of how we measure what we can never visit.

spotlights.name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a high-collared dress at Harvard who found the rule that measures galaxies.
spotlights.story_md: Leavitt studied at what became Radcliffe College, then volunteered at Harvard College Observatory in the 1890s. Edward Pickering hired her in 1902 to measure star brightness on photographic plates. By 1908 she had found 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds and noticed that the brighter ones pulsed more slowly. Her 1912 paper on 25 Cepheids made the rule exact. It was signed by Pickering, though its first line says it was prepared by Miss Leavitt. In 1924 the Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler wrote to nominate her for a Nobel Prize. She had died of cancer three years earlier, and the prize is never given to the dead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her period-luminosity rule is the rung that every modern measurement of the universe's size still leans on.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slow blink, big star. Leavitt's law fits in four words.

spotlights.name: The Harvard computers
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of women at desks with glass plates and ledgers, posed in front of the old observatory building.
spotlights.story_md: Before 'computer' meant a machine, it meant a person who did calculations. Edward Pickering, director of Harvard College Observatory from 1877, hired women to read the observatory's growing library of glass photographic plates, which eventually passed half a million. They were cheaper than men and, Pickering argued, more careful. The group included Williamina Fleming, a former maid in Pickering's house, who found the Horsehead Nebula; Annie Jump Cannon, who sorted around 350,000 stars into the O, B, A, F, G, K, M classes still taught today; and Leavitt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The data that unlocked distances came from underpaid women doing careful, repetitive work.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first computers wore long skirts and read glass.

sections.title: What the ladder is, in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
No tape measure reaches a star. So astronomers chain methods together. The first rung uses geometry, which works only close by. Each rung is used to calibrate the next one, which reaches farther but trusts more assumptions. That chain is the cosmic distance ladder.

Rung one is the size of the Earth and the distance to the Moon, measured with shadows and, now, lasers. Rung two is the distance to the Sun, the astronomical unit, fixed by planetary transits and then radar. Rung three is parallax: the tiny shift of a nearby star as Earth moves around the Sun. Rung four is standard candles: stars whose true brightness we can work out, such as Cepheids. Rung five is exploding white dwarfs, bright enough to see across billions of light years. At the top, the redshift of galaxies gives distance through the expansion of space itself.

The weakness is obvious. An error low on the ladder carries all the way up. When Hubble first measured the expansion rate in 1929, his ladder was off by a factor of about seven. The eight numbers below are the ones worth keeping.

spotlights.name: The parsec
spotlights.spot_it: The distance at which the Earth-Sun gap would look one arcsecond wide: 3.26 light years.
spotlights.story_md: Astronomers do not usually count in light years. They use the parsec, short for parallax-second. Imagine standing on a star and looking back at the Sun and Earth. If the gap between them looks as wide as one arcsecond, a 3,600th of a degree, you are one parsec away: about 31 trillion km, or 3.26 light years. The British astronomer Herbert Hall Turner suggested the name in 1913. Galaxies are measured in megaparsecs, millions of parsecs, which is why the expansion rate comes in kilometres per second per megaparsec.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the unit that comes straight out of the first geometric rung.
spotlights.memory_hook: One arcsecond of wobble, one parsec of distance.

sections.title: Shadows, eclipses and the first rung
sections.intro_md:
The ladder starts on the ground. Around 240 BCE a librarian in Alexandria used a shadow to measure the whole Earth. A few decades earlier, Aristarchus of Samos had used the shape of the half-lit Moon to argue that the Sun was enormously farther away than the Moon, and therefore enormously bigger. A century later Hipparchus used a solar eclipse seen from two places to estimate the Moon's distance in Earth radii.

None of these needed a telescope. They needed geometry, a clear sky and a willingness to trust a chain of reasoning. Their numbers ranged from very good to badly wrong, and the reasons are instructive: Eratosthenes' method was sound even though some of his assumptions were off, while Aristarchus' method was sound but needed an angle more precise than any eye could read.

spotlights.name: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
spotlights.spot_it: A stick, a shadow and two cities 5,000 stadia apart.
spotlights.story_md: Eratosthenes ran the Library of Alexandria. He had heard that at noon on the summer solstice in Syene, modern Aswan, the Sun shone straight down and vertical rods cast no shadow. In Alexandria, at the same moment, a rod's shadow showed the Sun was about 7.2 degrees off vertical: a fiftieth of a circle. If the cities were 5,000 stadia apart, Earth's circumference was about 250,000 stadia. How good was it? That depends on the length of a stadion, which scholars put between about 160 and 210 metres. Depending on which you choose, he was within 1% or about 15% of the truth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first rung: a size for the Earth, which every later baseline needs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fiftieth of a circle in a shadow, a whole planet in a sum.

spotlights.name: Aristarchus and the half Moon
spotlights.spot_it: A diagram of Sun, Earth and a half-lit Moon forming a right-angled triangle.
spotlights.story_md: When the Moon is exactly half lit, the angle at the Moon between Earth and Sun is a right angle. Aristarchus of Samos realised that if he measured the angle at Earth between the Moon and the Sun, simple trigonometry would give their relative distances. He read it as 87 degrees and concluded the Sun is 18 to 20 times farther away than the Moon. The true angle is about 89.85 degrees, which makes the ratio about 389. The method was flawless; the eye could not resolve the last fraction of a degree.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the ladder's oldest lesson: tiny angles, giant errors.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three degrees off, twenty times too close.

spotlights.name: Hipparchus and the eclipse of 190 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: The Greek astronomer with a globe, often shown in Renaissance paintings and on coins of Nicaea.
spotlights.story_md: Hipparchus worked on Rhodes and is credited with the first star catalogue in the Greek world and the discovery of the slow wobble of Earth's axis. For the Moon's distance he is thought to have used a solar eclipse that was total near the Hellespont but only partial in Alexandria. The difference showed how far the Moon shifts when seen from two places on Earth: its parallax. From that he worked out a distance in Earth radii, and later reconstructions put his range at roughly 60 to 67, against a true average of 60.3.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first parallax measurement, the same trick later used on stars.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same eclipse, two cities, one Moon distance.

sections.title: How far is the Sun
sections.intro_md:
By 1619 Johannes Kepler had found that a planet's orbital period squared is proportional to its distance from the Sun cubed. That gave astronomers a perfect scale model of the solar system: they knew Mars was about 1.52 times as far from the Sun as Earth. What they did not know was the size of the model in kilometres. Measure any one distance in the solar system and all the others follow.

The next 350 years were a hunt for that one number. Expeditions crossed oceans to time a black dot crossing the Sun. Some died. One man lost his wife, his estate and his legal existence. Then, in the early 1960s, radar bounced off Venus and settled the question in an afternoon. In 2012 the astronomers gave up measuring it altogether and simply defined it.

The Moon got the same treatment. Since 1969, reflectors left by astronauts have let observatories time laser pulses to the Moon and back, and the Earth-Moon distance is now known to about a millimetre.

spotlights.name: Cassini, Richer and Mars in 1672
spotlights.spot_it: Two observers, Paris and French Guiana, timing Mars against the same background stars.
spotlights.story_md: In 1672 Mars came unusually close to Earth. Giovanni Domenico Cassini stayed at the new Paris Observatory while Jean Richer sailed to Cayenne in French Guiana, roughly 7,000 km away. Each recorded Mars' position against nearby stars. The tiny difference between the two views, its parallax, gave Mars' distance, and Kepler's scale model turned that into the Sun's distance. Their result implied a solar parallax of about 9.5 arcseconds, or roughly 140 million km, within about 7% of the true value.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first measurement of the solar system in real units that was close to right.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paris and Cayenne, two eyes on one Mars.

spotlights.name: The transits of Venus
spotlights.spot_it: A small, perfectly round black dot crawling across the Sun's face over about six hours.
spotlights.story_md: Venus crosses the face of the Sun in pairs eight years apart, with more than a century between pairs. Edmond Halley proposed in 1716 that observers far apart on Earth could time the crossing and, from the difference, work out the Sun's distance. In 1761 and 1769 Britain, France and others sent hundreds of observers around the world. Jérôme Lalande combined the results in 1771: 153 million km, plus or minus a million. The great nuisance was the black drop effect, where Venus seems to stick to the Sun's edge like a drop of ink, smearing the timing by many seconds. The next transit is in December 2117.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was history's first global science project, aimed at one number.
spotlights.memory_hook: A black dot, a stopwatch and the whole solar system.

spotlights.name: Cook at Point Venus
spotlights.spot_it: A black-sand point on Tahiti with a lighthouse, where the Endeavour's crew built a small fort.
spotlights.story_md: James Cook's first Pacific voyage on HMS Endeavour was officially a Royal Society astronomy mission. He was to observe the 1769 transit from Tahiti, then open sealed orders, which sent him to search for a southern continent and led to his charting of New Zealand and eastern Australia. On 3 June, Cook and the astronomer Charles Green watched from a temporary fort on a spit now called Point Venus. The sky was clear. Even so, their contact times disagreed with each other by several seconds because of the black drop. Green died on the way home, as did many of the crew.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Science funded the voyage; empire followed it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cook went to Tahiti for a dot on the Sun.

spotlights.name: Guillaume Le Gentil, the unluckiest astronomer
spotlights.spot_it: A French astronomer who spent 11 years chasing two transits and saw neither.
spotlights.story_md: Le Gentil sailed for Pondicherry, the French post in India, to observe the 1761 transit. War with Britain intervened: Pondicherry fell, and on transit day he was still at sea, where a rolling deck made his timings useless. He decided to wait eight years for the next one. He chose Pondicherry again, built an observatory there and waited. On 4 June 1769 the morning was cloudy for exactly the hours of the transit; Manila, his alternative, had clear skies. He returned to France in 1771 to find he had been declared dead, his wife had remarried and his relatives had divided his estate. He won back his seat in the Academy, remarried and lived another 21 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His story shows what one number used to cost: decades, voyages and luck.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight years waiting, one cloud, declared dead.

spotlights.name: Radar echoes from Venus

where.label: Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex, California

spotlights.spot_it: A giant dish sending a pulse to Venus and timing the faint echo.
spotlights.story_md: Optical methods had reached their limit. In 1961 teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, using the Goldstone antennas in the California desert, and at MIT's Millstone Hill bounced radio pulses off Venus. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so timing the round trip gives the distance directly, and Kepler's laws turn that into the astronomical unit. The first results were good to a few hundred kilometres, and within a few years the AU was pinned far more tightly than any optical method had ever managed. In 2012, at its General Assembly in Beijing, the International Astronomical Union stopped measuring it and fixed it as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rung two went from centuries of expeditions to an echo.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shout at Venus, count the seconds, know the Sun.

spotlights.name: Lunar laser ranging
spotlights.spot_it: A small grey panel of glass corner-cubes sitting in the lunar dust beside bootprints.
spotlights.story_md: On 21 July 1969 the Apollo 11 crew set down a panel about 46 cm across holding 100 glass corner-cube reflectors. Each one sends light back exactly the way it came. Days later, on 1 August, Lick Observatory in California caught laser pulses returning from it. The challenge is brutal: a laser beam has spread to about 6.5 km wide by the time it hits the Moon, and of roughly 300 million billion photons sent, only a handful come back. Even so, the Earth-Moon distance is now measured to about a millimetre, which shows the Moon drifting away by about 3.8 cm a year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the bottom rung measured more precisely than anything above it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fire hundreds of quadrillions of photons, catch a few, measure a millimetre.

sections.title: The parallax race of 1838
sections.intro_md:
Hold a finger up at arm's length and blink one eye, then the other. The finger jumps against the background. That jump is parallax, and it is the only direct, purely geometric way to measure a star's distance. Instead of two eyes, astronomers use two positions of Earth six months apart, 300 million km apart.

The idea was ancient. In fact the failure to see any stellar parallax was one of the strongest arguments against a moving Earth: if we orbit the Sun, why don't the stars shift? The answer was that they do, but by less than one arcsecond, about the width of a coin seen from several kilometres. Telescopes of the 1700s could not see it.

By the 1830s three astronomers were closing in, each on a different star. Friedrich Bessel in Königsberg won, publishing in 1838. Thomas Henderson, who had the data first, and Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve published within months. After more than 2,000 years of searching, humans had the distance to a star.

data.observer: Thomas Henderson, Cape of Good Hope

spotlights.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel
spotlights.spot_it: A Prussian astronomer with a high collar and a sharp gaze, master of precise measurement.
spotlights.story_md: Bessel left school at 14 to work as a merchant's apprentice in Bremen and taught himself astronomy at night. He chose his target with care. Rather than the brightest star, he picked one that moved fastest across the sky, reasoning that fast-moving stars are probably close. Using a new heliometer built by Joseph von Fraunhofer's workshop, he measured 61 Cygni against two faint background stars over more than a year. In 1838 he announced a parallax of 0.314 arcseconds: about 10 light years. The modern figure is 11.4.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned the stars from points on a dome into objects at measurable distances.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bessel bet on the fastest star, not the brightest.

sections.title: Two satellites that remapped the stars
sections.intro_md:
From the ground, the atmosphere blurs star images to about an arcsecond. That made parallax reliable only out to about a hundred light years for most of the 20th century. To go farther, astronomers had to leave the air behind.

The European Space Agency's Hipparcos satellite, launched in 1989, measured the positions of about 118,000 stars to around a thousandth of an arcsecond. Its successor Gaia, launched in 2013, went a hundred times finer and measured nearly two billion objects. Together they turned the first stellar rung from a few hundred stars into a three-dimensional map of a large chunk of the Milky Way.

Gaia also measured the parallaxes of Cepheids directly, which matters because the whole upper ladder depends on knowing how bright a Cepheid really is. Gaia stopped observing in January 2025 and was switched off in March 2025, and its fourth data release is scheduled for December 2026.

rows.Gaia: About 0.01 to 0.03 milliarcseconds for bright stars

rows.Hipparcos: Stuck in an elongated transfer orbit after its motor failed

spotlights.name: Hipparcos
spotlights.spot_it: A squat hexagonal European satellite with a single telescope that looked in two directions at once.
spotlights.story_md: Its name is both an acronym, High Precision Parallax Collecting Satellite, and a nod to Hipparchus. Launched on an Ariane rocket in August 1989, it suffered a disaster on day one: its apogee motor never fired, leaving it in a looping transfer orbit instead of a fixed geostationary one. Engineers reworked the mission and it ran for more than three years anyway, sweeping the sky with a mirror that combined two fields of view 58 degrees apart. The 1997 catalogue held 118,218 stars with parallaxes near a milliarcsecond, and the Tycho-2 catalogue added 2.5 million less precise ones.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made the first rung precise for thousands of stars instead of hundreds.
spotlights.memory_hook: A satellite in the wrong orbit still remapped the sky.

spotlights.name: Gaia
spotlights.spot_it: A spinning top hat in space: a round sunshield 10 metres across with a box of telescopes on top.
spotlights.story_md: Gaia rotated slowly at the L2 point, 1.5 million km from Earth, sweeping two telescopes across the sky onto a focal plane of 106 CCDs, nearly a billion pixels. Each star crossed it about 70 times over the mission. For bright stars Gaia's parallaxes reach a few millionths of an arcsecond, roughly the width of a human hair seen from 1,000 km. Its third data release in 2022 held about 1.8 billion sources. Gaia ended science observations on 15 January 2025 and was switched off on 27 March 2025, parked in an orbit around the Sun. Data Release 4, covering 66 months, is planned for 2 December 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anchors Cepheid brightness directly, the rung everything above depends on.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hair's width from a thousand kilometres, for a billion stars.

spotlights.name: The Pleiades distance fight
spotlights.spot_it: The Seven Sisters, a tight, blue-white cluster in Taurus wrapped in faint dust.
spotlights.story_md: The Pleiades, known in India as Krittika, is the nearest bright star cluster and a test bed for stellar models. Hipparcos placed it at about 120 parsecs. Nearly every other method, from stellar models to ground-based parallax, said about 133. A 10% gap sounds small, but it meant either the satellite had a hidden error or our understanding of young stars was wrong. In 2014 radio astronomers used a network of telescopes spread across continents to measure parallaxes of a few cluster stars directly: 136.2 ± 1.2 parsecs. Gaia later agreed. The fault was in how Hipparcos' measurements had been combined for stars close together on the sky.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that even geometric rungs carry hidden systematic errors.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Seven Sisters caught a satellite out.

sections.title: Stars that tell you their wattage
sections.intro_md:
Parallax runs out. Even Gaia's precision fades a few tens of thousands of light years away, still inside our own galaxy. Beyond that, astronomers need a standard candle: an object whose true brightness can be worked out from something other than its distance.

The physics is the inverse square law. A light twice as far away looks four times fainter. If you know how much light a star gives off and you measure how much reaches you, the distance follows. Astronomers express this with magnitudes, a backwards scale where bigger numbers mean fainter, and five magnitudes mean a factor of exactly 100 in brightness.

Cepheids are the classic candle. They are yellow supergiants, up to 100,000 times as luminous as the Sun, that swell and shrink on a regular beat of 1 to 100 days. Leavitt's law says the longer the beat, the brighter the star. Calibrate the law with a few Cepheids of known distance, and every Cepheid in every galaxy close enough to see one becomes a measuring stick. The catch is in that word calibrate, and in the dust between us and the star.

spotlights.name: John Goodricke
spotlights.spot_it: A deaf teenager in York who found the first Cepheid and explained eclipsing stars.
spotlights.story_md: Goodricke lost his hearing in early childhood and was educated at Thomas Braidwood's school for deaf pupils in Edinburgh. Back in York he observed the sky with his neighbour Edward Pigott. In 1782, aged 18, he timed the regular dimming of Algol and proposed it was being eclipsed by a dark companion, earning the Royal Society's Copley Medal. Pigott then found that Eta Aquilae varied, and Goodricke found the same in Delta Cephei, the star that gave the whole class its name. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society on 16 April 1786. He died of pneumonia four days later, aged 21, without hearing the news.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first Cepheid was found by a deaf 20-year-old, and the law that uses it by a deaf woman.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two deaf astronomers bracket the Cepheid story.

spotlights.name: Delta Cephei and the Eddington valve
spotlights.spot_it: A naked-eye star in Cepheus that brightens and fades every 5 days, 8 hours and 48 minutes.
spotlights.story_md: Delta Cephei's brightness rises fast and falls slowly, a sawtooth light curve that is the Cepheid signature. Why does it pulse? Arthur Eddington suggested a valve. Deep in the star's outer layers, helium can lose one or both of its electrons. Doubly ionised helium is more opaque, so it traps heat, the layer swells and cools, the helium recaptures an electron, becomes more transparent, lets heat out and falls back. Bigger, brighter stars have larger envelopes that take longer to complete this cycle, which is why period tracks luminosity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The physics explains why Leavitt's rule works and when it might not.
spotlights.memory_hook: A star that breathes through a helium valve.

spotlights.name: Polaris, the disputed Cepheid
spotlights.spot_it: The North Star, the end of the Little Dipper's handle, which pulses gently every four days.
spotlights.story_md: Polaris is the nearest Cepheid to Earth, so its distance should be a cornerstone. It turned into a fight instead. Hipparcos put it about 432 light years away. David Turner and colleagues argued from 2004 to 2013 for about 323 light years, using a faint companion and a possible star cluster. Floor van Leeuwen, who reduced the Hipparcos data, replied that the data could not support that. A Hubble Space Telescope parallax of its companion in 2018 came out even farther, and Gaia's third data release puts the companion Polaris B at about 446 light years. A 30% disagreement over the best-known star in the northern sky shows how hard even near rungs can be.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If the nearest Cepheid is uncertain, so is every calibration that uses it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Even the North Star argued about its address.

spotlights.name: RS Puppis and its light echo
spotlights.spot_it: A bright star inside nested rings of glowing dust, like a target, in a Hubble image.
spotlights.story_md: RS Puppis is a Cepheid that pulses every 41.4 days and sits inside a cloud of dust. Each time it brightens, the pulse of light travels outward and lights up the dust in turn, so rings of brightness appear to ripple out. That is a light echo. By matching the timing of the echo at different points in the cloud to the star's known pulse, a team led by Pierre Kervella worked out the geometry and got a distance of about 6,500 light years, with an uncertainty near 1%.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare purely geometric distance to a Cepheid beyond parallax range.
spotlights.memory_hook: The star's pulse ripples through its own dust like sonar.

sections.title: The night the universe got bigger
sections.intro_md:
In 1920 nobody knew whether the Milky Way was the whole universe. Spiral nebulae, faint pinwheels like the one in Andromeda, might be small clouds inside our galaxy or entire galaxies far beyond it. On 26 April 1920, in Washington, Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis argued it out in what was later called the Great Debate.

Shapley had used Cepheid-like stars to show that the Milky Way was enormous, about 300,000 light years across by his count, with the Sun far from its centre. He was right about the Sun and the centre, too high on the size, and wrong about the nebulae. Curtis argued for 'island universes' and was mostly right about the nebulae for partly wrong reasons. Neither had a way to settle it.

Three years later Edwin Hubble did, using the largest telescope on Earth and Leavitt's law. One photographic plate, with one word scrawled on it, ended the argument.

spotlights.name: Shapley vs Curtis

where.label: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Washington, D.C.

spotlights.spot_it: Two astronomers, one hall in the Smithsonian's natural history building, the size of the universe on the table.
spotlights.story_md: The debate was less dramatic than its name, two talks to the National Academy of Sciences. Shapley's case rested partly on Adriaan van Maanen, who claimed to have seen spiral nebulae rotating over a few years. If spirals were huge and distant, their edges would be moving faster than light; therefore they had to be small and near. Van Maanen's measurements were wrong; the effect was too small to see in a human lifetime. Curtis pointed to novae in spirals, which looked much fainter than novae in our galaxy, so the spirals must be very far away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It framed the question that the distance ladder was about to answer.
spotlights.memory_hook: One man said one galaxy; the other said many. Many won.

spotlights.name: Hubble's 'VAR!' plate
spotlights.spot_it: A glass negative of Andromeda with a star marked 'N', crossed out and relabelled 'VAR!'
spotlights.story_md: Hubble was hunting for novae in Andromeda with the 100-inch telescope. On one plate he marked three new spots with N for nova. Comparing it with older plates, he saw that one of them brightened and faded on a regular cycle of about 31 days. It was not a nova. It was a Cepheid. He crossed out the N and wrote VAR!, for variable, exclamation mark included. Using Leavitt's law he put Andromeda about 900,000 light years away, far beyond Shapley's Milky Way. The plate, H335H, is kept at the Carnegie Observatories in Pasadena. The star, M31-V1, has been followed by amateurs ever since.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One star made the universe a place of galaxies.
spotlights.memory_hook: N for nova became VAR! for the universe.

spotlights.name: The Hooker 100-inch telescope
spotlights.spot_it: A giant open-frame telescope in a white dome on Mount Wilson, its mirror a 2.5 metre disc of green bottle glass.
spotlights.story_md: Funded by the Los Angeles businessman John D. Hooker and the Carnegie Institution, the telescope's mirror, weighing more than 4 tonnes, was cast in France from wine-bottle glass. It was full of bubbles, and George Ellery Hale nearly rejected it. Ground and polished in Pasadena, it worked, and from 1917 to 1949 it was the largest telescope in the world. Its light-gathering power let Hubble see individual stars in Andromeda.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without enough aperture to see single stars in other galaxies, the ladder stopped at the Milky Way.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wine-bottle glass found the other galaxies.

spotlights.name: The Andromeda Galaxy
spotlights.spot_it: A faint, elongated smudge in Andromeda, visible to the naked eye from a dark site in autumn.
spotlights.story_md: Andromeda is the most distant thing most people can see without a telescope. The light reaching you tonight left it about 2.5 million years ago, when early members of our genus were living in Africa. It is a spiral galaxy somewhat larger than the Milky Way, at about 765 kiloparsecs. Hubble's first estimate was less than half that, because his Cepheid calibration was off; Walter Baade fixed that in the 1950s. Andromeda is one of the few galaxies moving towards us, at about 110 km per second relative to the Milky Way, a reminder that redshift is only a distance gauge far away, where expansion dominates local motion.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the stepping stone between our galaxy and every other.
spotlights.memory_hook: The farthest thing your eye can see, 2.5 million years old.

sections.title: Everything is running away
sections.intro_md:
Distances alone do not make a cosmology. The other half came from light split into a spectrum. Dark lines from elements sit at known wavelengths; if a galaxy is moving away, the lines slide towards red. That shift, the redshift, gives a speed without needing a distance at all.

From 1912 Vesto Slipher at Lowell Observatory in Arizona found that most spiral nebulae were moving away fast. In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, showed that Einstein's equations allowed an expanding universe and that speed should grow with distance. In 1929 Edwin Hubble, with Milton Humason, plotted velocity against Cepheid-based distance for a couple of dozen galaxies and found a straight line. The slope is the Hubble constant, H0: how many kilometres per second of recession you gain per megaparsec of distance.

Hubble's slope was about 500. It implied a universe roughly 2 billion years old, younger than the rocks of Earth. The fix came from the ladder, not the theory: his distances were too small. For the next 70 years astronomers argued over whether H0 was 50 or 100, a factor of two in the size and age of everything.

visual.title: The Hubble constant over the decades (km/s per Mpc)

spotlights.name: Vesto Slipher
spotlights.spot_it: A careful Indiana-born spectroscopist at Lowell Observatory, working with a 24-inch refractor in a wooden dome.
spotlights.story_md: Percival Lowell asked Slipher to take spectra of spiral nebulae, which he thought might be forming solar systems. These were brutally faint: one spectrum of Andromeda in 1912 took exposures spread over several nights. It showed Andromeda approaching at about 300 km per second, the fastest speed then measured for anything in the sky. By 1917 Slipher had 25 spirals, and most were receding, some at over 1,000 km per second. Those were far too fast for anything bound to the Milky Way. Slipher's velocities were the raw material for Hubble's law, and his name is often left out of it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The speeds came first; the distances arrived later.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slipher clocked the speeds; Hubble got the credit.

spotlights.name: Georges Lemaître
spotlights.spot_it: A Belgian Catholic priest in a clerical collar standing beside Einstein and Millikan in a famous 1933 photograph.
spotlights.story_md: Lemaître, a priest and a physicist trained at Cambridge and MIT, published in 1927, in French, in a little-read Belgian journal, a solution of Einstein's equations for an expanding universe. Using Slipher's speeds and Hubble's early distances he estimated the expansion rate, two years before Hubble's paper. Einstein reportedly told him his mathematics was correct but his physics abominable. When the paper was translated into English in 1931, the paragraph with the expansion rate was missing. Conspiracy theories blamed Hubble's allies; in 2011 the astrophysicist Mario Livio found letters showing Lemaître cut it himself, thinking it out of date.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He predicted and measured expansion first, and in 2018 the law was renamed to include him.
spotlights.memory_hook: A priest beat Hubble by two years and left his number out.

spotlights.name: Hubble's 1929 diagram
spotlights.spot_it: A scatter of dots rising to the right, velocity against distance, with a straight line through them.
spotlights.story_md: The paper, 'A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae', appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. It is only six pages. The data are scrappy: distances for the nearest galaxies from Cepheids, for others from their brightest stars, and for the farthest from their total brightness. The scatter is large and the slope, about 500 km per second per megaparsec, was about seven times too steep. But the pattern was right, and later spectra by Milton Humason, a former mule driver at Mount Wilson, pushed it out to far greater distances.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a pile of speeds into the expanding universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six pages, one line, the whole universe moving.

spotlights.name: Walter Baade and the blackout
spotlights.spot_it: A German astronomer working at Mount Wilson during the Second World War while Los Angeles went dark.
spotlights.story_md: Baade was German, and when the United States entered the war he was barred from war work, so he kept observing. Wartime blackouts dimmed Los Angeles below Mount Wilson, and in 1943 and 1944 he used the darker skies to resolve the centre of Andromeda into individual stars for the first time. He saw two kinds of star populations, young and old, and later realised there were two kinds of Cepheid too, with different brightness for the same period. Hubble had calibrated with the wrong kind. At the International Astronomical Union meeting in Rome in 1952 Baade announced that the extragalactic distance scale was about twice as large as thought.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One correction doubled the size and age of the universe overnight.
spotlights.memory_hook: The blackout made the universe twice as big.

sections.title: More than one way up
sections.intro_md:
A ladder with one leg wobbles. Since the 1990s astronomers have added independent anchors and candles so that no single star type decides everything.

The anchors are geometric distances that skip parallax: pairs of stars eclipsing each other in the Large Magellanic Cloud, water vapour glowing like a laser around a black hole in the galaxy NGC 4258, and the light echo of a ring around a supernova. Each gives a distance to a whole galaxy, where many Cepheids can be calibrated at once.

The new candles are red giants at a precise stage of life, and a class of carbon-rich giant stars, both easier to see through dust than Cepheids. Farther out, the spin of spiral galaxies and the graininess of elliptical galaxies give rougher distances.

The point is cross-checking. If Cepheids and red giants, calibrated on the same anchors, give the same distance to the same galaxy, the ladder is probably sound. When they disagree by a few percent, that becomes front-page science.

visual.title: Where the geometric anchors are measured

pins.label: Gaia parallaxes from L2 (Milky Way stars)
Las Campanas, Chile: LMC eclipsing binaries
VLBA dishes across the US: NGC 4258 masers

spotlights.name: Eclipsing binaries in the Large Magellanic Cloud
spotlights.spot_it: A bright satellite galaxy in the southern sky, home to 20 carefully chosen pairs of eclipsing giant stars.
spotlights.story_md: When two stars orbit edge-on, they take turns blocking each other. The length of each eclipse, combined with the stars' orbital speeds from their spectra, gives their physical sizes in kilometres. Their colour tells you how bright each unit of surface is, which gives their apparent size in the sky. Physical size divided by apparent size is distance. A team led by Grzegorz Pietrzyński spent many years monitoring 20 such pairs of cool giant stars. Their 2019 paper in Nature gave the Large Magellanic Cloud's distance as 49.59 kiloparsecs, about 162,000 light years, with a total uncertainty of 1.1%.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best anchor outside our galaxy and does not use parallax at all.
spotlights.memory_hook: Watch two stars hide behind each other; get a galaxy's distance.

spotlights.name: The water masers of NGC 4258
spotlights.spot_it: A spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici with a thin disc of glowing water vapour orbiting its central black hole.
spotlights.story_md: A maser is a laser in microwaves. In the galaxy NGC 4258, also called Messier 106, water molecules in a gas disc around a black hole of about 40 million Suns amplify radio waves at 22 gigahertz into tight, bright spots. Radio telescopes linked across thousands of kilometres can map those spots and their speeds. Spots on the near side drift across the sky over years, and their acceleration shows how fast they orbit. Comparing the speed in kilometres per second with the drift in angle gives the disc's real size and so the galaxy's distance: 7.58 megaparsecs, about 24.7 million light years, to about 1.5%.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the only geometric anchor beyond the Local Group used to calibrate Cepheids.
spotlights.memory_hook: Water lasers orbiting a black hole measure the galaxy.

spotlights.name: The tip of the red giant branch
spotlights.spot_it: A sharp upper edge on a graph of star colour against brightness, where red giants stop climbing.
spotlights.story_md: As a Sun-like star ages, its core runs out of hydrogen and it swells into a red giant, growing brighter as its helium core grows. When the core reaches a critical mass, about half the Sun's, the helium ignites in a sudden flash. Because the trigger is almost the same for every such star, the brightest red giants all peak at nearly the same luminosity, especially in near-infrared light. In a galaxy's outer halo, plot thousands of stars, find where the red giants stop, and you have a standard candle. Red giants are old and live in dust-free halos, which avoids the crowding and dust that complicate Cepheids.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the main independent check on Cepheids, and it gives a slightly lower H0.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every red giant hits the same ceiling, then flashes.

sections.title: Exploding white dwarfs and a speeding universe
sections.intro_md:
Cepheids are bright, but not bright enough to see in galaxies billions of light years away. For that astronomers need something that briefly outshines an entire galaxy. Type Ia supernovae do.

A white dwarf is the hot, Earth-sized core left when a star like the Sun dies. If it gains mass from a companion, or merges with another white dwarf, and approaches about 1.4 times the Sun's mass, carbon ignites everywhere at once and the star blows apart completely. At peak it shines about 5 billion times brighter than the Sun. Because the explosions happen near the same mass, they are similar in brightness, and in 1993 Mark Phillips showed how to correct for the differences: brighter ones fade more slowly.

In 1998 and 1999 two rival teams used them to measure how the expansion had changed over time. They expected slowing down. Distant supernovae were fainter than expected: the expansion is speeding up. Whatever drives it was named dark energy, and it makes up about two thirds of the universe's contents. That discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

visual.title: What the universe is made of (Planck 2018)

spotlights.name: Type Ia supernovae
spotlights.spot_it: A new point of light at the edge of a galaxy that rivals the galaxy's whole core, then fades over weeks.
spotlights.story_md: The spectrum gives them away: no hydrogen lines, but a strong silicon line. They happen roughly once a century in a galaxy like ours, so astronomers watch thousands of galaxies to catch them. The rule that makes them usable, the Phillips relation, came from the Calán/Tololo survey in Chile: measure how fast the light drops in the 15 days after peak, and you can correct the peak brightness to within about 7% in distance. To be useful for H0, each needs a calibration: a supernova in a galaxy close enough to also have Cepheids or red giants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They carry the ladder from tens of millions of light years to billions.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dying white dwarf is a lighthouse with a known wattage.

spotlights.name: SN 2014J, found in a class

where.label: University of London Observatory, Mill Hill

spotlights.spot_it: A new star in the Cigar Galaxy, spotted from a London observatory between rain showers.
spotlights.story_md: On a cloudy evening Steve Fossey was teaching four undergraduates at the University of London Observatory in Mill Hill to use a CCD camera. With clouds closing in, he pointed the telescope at the bright galaxy M82 for a quick demonstration. A star sat there that was not on older images. The students checked it was not an instrument fault, then reported it. It was a Type Ia supernova 11.5 million light years away, the nearest since 1972, and within days telescopes worldwide and in space were on it. It was close enough to test how dust inside a galaxy dims and reddens these candles, a key error source for the ladder.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nearby Type Ia events are rare chances to test the candle in detail.
spotlights.memory_hook: A teaching session caught the nearest exploding white dwarf in 42 years.

spotlights.name: The accelerating universe
spotlights.spot_it: Three physicists sharing the 2011 Nobel stage: Perlmutter from Berkeley, Schmidt from Canberra, Riess from Baltimore.
spotlights.story_md: Two teams raced to measure how much gravity was slowing the expansion. Saul Perlmutter led the Supernova Cosmology Project from Berkeley; Brian Schmidt led the High-Z Supernova Search Team, with Adam Riess doing much of the analysis. Both found distant supernovae about 10 to 25% fainter than a slowing universe would allow. Riess, then in his late twenties, reportedly checked his code for weeks, convinced he had made a mistake. The High-Z paper came out in 1998, Perlmutter's in 1999. The universe started speeding up a few billion years ago. Perlmutter received half the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics; Schmidt and Riess shared the other half.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It revealed dark energy, the largest single ingredient of the universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: The brakes were the accelerator.

sections.title: Measuring without a ladder
sections.intro_md:
Because every rung inherits the errors below it, astronomers prize methods that skip the ladder entirely. There are four main ones.

The cosmic microwave background is light from 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Its pattern of hot and cold spots, combined with the standard cosmological model, predicts what H0 should be today. Baryon acoustic oscillations are frozen sound waves from the same era that left a preferred spacing between galaxies, about 490 million light years, which works as a standard ruler. Gravitational waves from colliding neutron stars carry their own distance in the shape of the signal: these are 'standard sirens'. And when a galaxy bends the light of a distant supernova into several images, the delays between them depend on H0.

There is a subtlety. The CMB and BAO numbers depend on assuming the standard model of the universe is right. If something new happened early on, those methods would give the wrong answer while the ladder gave the right one. That is the heart of the current argument.

spotlights.name: Planck and the baby picture
spotlights.spot_it: A mottled oval map of the whole sky in blue and orange: the oldest light in the universe.
spotlights.story_md: The European Space Agency's Planck satellite launched on 14 May 2009 alongside Herschel and mapped the cosmic microwave background until 2013. Its detectors were cooled to a tenth of a degree above absolute zero to sense temperature differences of millionths of a degree. The sizes of the spots in that map are set by sound waves in the early universe, whose physics is well understood. Fit the standard model to the pattern and out comes the expansion rate today: 67.4 ± 0.5 km per second per megaparsec, published in 2018. That is a prediction, not a direct measurement of nearby galaxies, which is exactly why the gap with the ladder matters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It sets the early-universe side of the Hubble tension.
spotlights.memory_hook: The baby picture says the universe should be growing slower than it is.

spotlights.name: Baryon acoustic oscillations
spotlights.spot_it: A faint excess of galaxy pairs about 490 million light years apart, the echo of sound in the early universe.
spotlights.story_md: For its first 380,000 years the universe was a hot plasma where sound waves rippled outward from denser clumps. When the plasma cooled into neutral gas, the ripples froze. Each left a shell of slightly extra matter at a fixed radius, about 150 megaparsecs today, and galaxies later formed slightly more often at that separation. Measure the angle that ruler spans at different distances and you trace the universe's expansion history. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the 2dF survey detected it in 2005. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, which uses 5,000 robot-positioned optical fibres on the Mayall telescope in Arizona, now maps tens of millions of galaxies to measure it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the standard ruler that links the CMB to the modern universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Big Bang's sound wave is printed in where galaxies sit.

spotlights.name: GW170817, the first standard siren
spotlights.spot_it: A new dot in the elliptical galaxy NGC 4993, the glow of two neutron stars that collided 130 million years ago.
spotlights.story_md: In 1986 the physicist Bernard Schutz pointed out that gravitational waves encode their source's true strength, so their loudness gives distance directly, no ladder needed. On 17 August 2017 the LIGO and Virgo detectors caught two neutron stars spiralling together. About 1.7 seconds after the merger, a burst of gamma rays arrived, and within hours telescopes found the glowing debris in NGC 4993, about 40 megaparsecs away, giving a redshift. Distance from the waves plus speed from the galaxy gave H0 = 70, with an uncertainty of about plus 12 and minus 8. The collision is estimated to have forged several Earth masses of gold and platinum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It opened a ladder-free route to H0 that improves with every new event.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spacetime rang like a bell, and the bell gave the distance.

spotlights.name: Supernova Refsdal, the rerun
spotlights.spot_it: Four images of one supernova arranged in a cross around a galaxy in a cluster, plus a fifth that appeared a year later.
spotlights.story_md: In 1964 the Norwegian astronomer Sjur Refsdal proposed that a supernova seen through a gravitational lens would appear several times, with delays that depend on the universe's scale. In November 2014 Hubble saw exactly that: a supernova behind the galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, split into four images. Models predicted another image would appear about a year later in a different spot. It did, in December 2015, one of the few times astronomers have predicted a supernova's appearance in advance. Patrick Kelly's team used the delays to measure H0 at 66.6, with an uncertainty of about plus 4 and minus 3, published in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Lensing gives a one-step distance scale that bypasses the ladder.
spotlights.memory_hook: The same explosion, shown twice, a year apart.

sections.title: The Hubble tension
sections.intro_md:
Here is the puzzle. Measure H0 with the ladder, from parallax to Cepheids to supernovae, and you get about 73 km per second per megaparsec. Predict it from the cosmic microwave background with the standard model, and you get about 67.4. The difference sounds small. It is about 8%, and both sides now claim uncertainties near 1%. The SH0ES team put the disagreement at five standard deviations in 2022, the level physicists treat as a discovery.

There are two kinds of explanation. One is a hidden error somewhere in the ladder: Cepheids blended with neighbouring stars in crowded images, dust, or a flaw in a calibration. The other is new physics: something in the early universe, such as a brief burst of extra dark energy, that changes the CMB prediction. A third, quieter camp argues that different candles give different answers and the truth may sit in between.

The James Webb Space Telescope, which sees in infrared and resolves crowded fields, was the test everyone waited for. Both main teams have used it. They still disagree, and their disagreement is now the most interesting number in cosmology.

visual.title: Recent estimates of H0 (km/s per Mpc)

spotlights.name: SH0ES and Adam Riess
spotlights.spot_it: The team whose acronym hides the symbol H0: Supernovae and H0 for the Equation of State.
spotlights.story_md: After the dark energy discovery, Adam Riess set out to nail H0 with the fewest, cleanest steps: geometric anchors, then Cepheids in galaxies that also hosted Type Ia supernovae, then supernovae far away. Every step uses the same instruments where possible, to cancel errors. By 2022 the team had Cepheids in the hosts of 42 supernovae and reported H0 = 73.04 ± 1.04, the first measurement with a 1 km per second per megaparsec uncertainty. Critics suspected that Hubble's blurry images blended Cepheids with neighbours. JWST's sharper infrared images from 2023 onward showed the same distances. Riess' view: the ladder is fine, and the model needs fixing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the strongest ladder measurement and the main source of the tension.
spotlights.memory_hook: SH0ES says 73, and JWST backs it.

spotlights.name: Wendy Freedman and the CCHP
spotlights.spot_it: The astronomer who led the Hubble Key Project and now argues the tension may be smaller than claimed.
spotlights.story_md: Wendy Freedman led the Hubble Space Telescope Key Project that gave 72 ± 8 in 2001. Her Chicago-Carnegie Hubble Program now prefers red giant stars and carbon-rich giants to Cepheids, arguing they are simpler and less affected by dust and crowding. Using JWST and Hubble, the team reported H0 = 70.39 in a 2025 paper, with a total uncertainty of about 2. That sits between the two camps and is consistent with the CMB value within the errors. SH0ES replies that the CCHP's supernova sample is small and that, analysed together, the methods agree near 72 to 73. A SH0ES analysis in late 2024 that used JWST data from both teams' programmes found 72.6 ± 2.0.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why some astronomers still think the tension could be a measurement problem.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same telescope, different stars, two numbers.

spotlights.name: The James Webb Space Telescope
spotlights.spot_it: A golden honeycomb mirror of 18 hexagons above a five-layer silver sunshield the size of a tennis court.
spotlights.story_md: JWST's 6.5 metre mirror and infrared cameras matter for the ladder for two reasons. Infrared light passes through dust that dims and reddens Cepheids in visible light. And its sharper images separate a Cepheid from the crowd of stars around it in a distant spiral arm, which Hubble sometimes could not. Webb has also detected red giant tips and carbon stars in supernova host galaxies. So far its results have not made the tension go away: Cepheid distances from Webb match Hubble's. What remains in dispute is which calibrators and which supernova samples to use.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was built partly to settle questions like this one, and it has sharpened rather than ended the argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: Webb looked through the dust and the gap was still there.

sections.title: The India connection
sections.intro_md:
India's link to the distance ladder runs from the fifth century to the 2030s. Aryabhata argued in 499 CE that the Earth spins, which removes the need for a whirling sky and is the first step towards thinking of the stars as distant suns. In the 19th century the Madras Observatory was the leading observatory in British Asia, and its director Norman Pogson defined the magnitude scale that every distance calculation still uses. The 1874 transit of Venus brought European expeditions to Indian soil.

In the 20th century a young physicist from Madras, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, worked out the mass limit that makes Type Ia supernovae roughly uniform, which is why they can be used as standard candles at all. In the 21st, India placed a laser reflector on the Moon with Chandrayaan-3 and is building a gravitational wave detector in Maharashtra that will help pin down standard sirens.

spotlights.name: Aryabhata
spotlights.spot_it: The mathematician-astronomer of Kusumapura, often shown as a seated statue in a robe, whose name went on India's first satellite.
spotlights.story_md: Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya at 23, according to the text itself. He stated that the Earth turns on its axis and that the apparent westward motion of the stars is an effect of that turning, like the shore seeming to move to someone in a boat. He gave the sidereal day as 23 hours, 56 minutes and about 4.1 seconds, against a modern 4.09. He also gave a size for the Earth in yojanas; converted with a common yojana value it comes close to the modern circumference, but the yojana's length is uncertain, so treat that match with care.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made the Earth, not the sky, the thing that moves, the first step to stars as distant suns.
spotlights.memory_hook: The boat moves, not the shore.

spotlights.name: Norman Pogson and the 2.512 rule
spotlights.spot_it: An English astronomer who ran the Madras Observatory for 30 years and fixed the brightness scale astronomers still use.
spotlights.story_md: Greek astronomers ranked stars from first magnitude, the brightest, to sixth, the faintest visible. In 1856 Pogson proposed making it exact: five magnitudes equal a factor of 100 in brightness, so each step is the fifth root of 100, about 2.512. That rule underlies the distance modulus, the equation that turns the gap between how bright a star looks and how bright it is into distance. In 1861 he took up the post of Government Astronomer at Madras. That year he discovered an asteroid from Madras and named it 67 Asia, the first found from the continent. His daughter Isis worked as his assistant from 1873 and was later admitted to the Royal Astronomical Society.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every standard candle calculation uses his scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five steps, a hundred times: Pogson's ratio from Madras.

spotlights.name: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
spotlights.spot_it: A slim young man in a suit from Madras who worked out, on a ship to England, how heavy a white dwarf can be.
spotlights.story_md: In 1930, aged 19, Chandrasekhar sailed from Madras to study at Cambridge. On the voyage he combined relativity with quantum physics and found that a white dwarf cannot support itself above a certain mass, now put at about 1.4 times the Sun's. In 1935 Arthur Eddington mocked the idea in public at the Royal Astronomical Society, and Chandrasekhar moved his work to Chicago. The limit is why Type Ia supernovae are similar: the white dwarfs explode near the same mass. He shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics, and NASA named its Chandra X-ray Observatory after him in 1999.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His limit is the physics that makes the top rung's candles roughly standard.
spotlights.memory_hook: A shipboard calculation sets the wattage of exploding stars.

spotlights.name: Chandrayaan-3's laser reflector
spotlights.spot_it: A palm-sized dome of eight glass corner-cubes on top of India's Vikram lander near the lunar south pole.
spotlights.story_md: When Vikram landed at the spot now called Shiv Shakti Point, it carried a small passive instrument from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center: the Laser Retroreflector Array, eight corner-cube reflectors on a hemisphere, weighing about 20 grams. It needs no power and should work for decades. On 12 December 2023 NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter fired its laser altimeter at it from about 100 km away and caught the reflection, the first time a laser had been bounced off a reflector on the Moon from lunar orbit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It extends the ladder's bottom rung to a new spot on the Moon.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty grams of glass on Vikram, pinged from orbit.

spotlights.name: LIGO-India
spotlights.spot_it: Two 4 km concrete tubes at right angles on the Deccan plateau, built to the same design as the American LIGO detectors.
spotlights.story_md: LIGO-India is a third detector of the LIGO network, near Aundha Nagnath in Hingoli district, Maharashtra. The Union Cabinet approved it in April 2023 at about Rs 2,600 crore, with IUCAA Pune, the Institute for Plasma Research and the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology leading, and the United States supplying detector hardware. Why it matters for distances: two or three detectors locate a merger only to a broad patch of sky. Adding a widely separated site sharpens that patch, which makes it far easier to find the host galaxy and so turn a gravitational wave into a standard siren. Completion is planned for about 2030; large science projects often slip.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It will make India part of the ladder-free route to H0.
spotlights.memory_hook: A detector in Hingoli to hear the universe's expansion.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Myth: a light year is a unit of time. Fact: it is a distance, the 9.46 trillion km light travels in a year.

Myth: Hubble discovered the expanding universe alone. Fact: Slipher measured the speeds, Lemaître derived and estimated the expansion first, and Humason took many of the spectra. In 2018 the IAU voted to recommend calling it the Hubble-Lemaître law.

Myth: most of the stars you see are already dead. Fact: nearly all naked-eye stars are within a few thousand light years, and stars live millions to billions of years. The chance any given one has died in the meantime is tiny.

Myth: nothing can recede faster than light, so the universe cannot be bigger than its age in light years. Fact: space itself expands. The observable universe is about 46 billion light years in radius though it is 13.8 billion years old, and very distant galaxies recede faster than light without breaking relativity.

Myth: redshift alone tells you distance. Fact: only far away. Nearby, galaxies' own motions dominate; Andromeda is approaching.

Myth: the Hubble tension means the Big Bang is wrong. Fact: both sides assume a Big Bang. The fight is over a detail of the model, or an error in a measurement.

sections.title: What is happening now, 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
The ladder is having its busiest decade since the 1920s. Gaia finished observing in January 2025 and was switched off on 27 March 2025; its fourth data release, based on 66 months of data, is scheduled for 2 December 2026, and will sharpen the parallaxes of Milky Way Cepheids. The Wendy Freedman team published its JWST red giant value of 70.39 in 2025, and in April 2026 a community report from the H0 Distance Network combined many local methods into 73.50 ± 0.81, firming up the high side.

On the early-universe side, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope's final data, released in March 2025, again pointed to about 68. The same month DESI released its second data set, strengthening hints that dark energy is weakening over time, one of the few new-physics ideas that could touch the tension.

New machines are arriving. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory showed its first images on 23 June 2025 and began its ten-year survey in mid 2026; it will find millions of supernovae. NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on 30 August 2026. And a 2025 study found only about a 50% chance that the Milky Way and Andromeda will merge in the next 10 billion years.

spotlights.name: DESI and the weakening of dark energy
spotlights.spot_it: A 4-metre telescope dome on Kitt Peak where 5,000 robotic fibres swivel into place in minutes.
spotlights.story_md: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument measures the redshifts of millions of galaxies and quasars to map baryon acoustic oscillations across 11 billion years. Its first-year results in April 2024 and its second data release on 19 March 2025 both preferred a model in which dark energy is not constant but weakening, with a significance of roughly 2.8 to 4.2 standard deviations depending on which supernova sample is added. That is not yet a discovery. If it holds, the standard model behind the CMB value of H0 would need revising, which could change the terms of the Hubble tension too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the strongest current hint that the cosmological model itself may need to change.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five thousand robot fibres say dark energy may be fading.

spotlights.name: Vera C. Rubin Observatory
spotlights.spot_it: A boxy white building on a Chilean ridge holding the largest digital camera ever built for astronomy, 3,200 megapixels.
spotlights.story_md: Named after the American astronomer whose galaxy rotation measurements built the case for dark matter, Rubin sits on Cerro Pachón at 2,682 metres. Its 8.4 metre telescope and 3.2 gigapixel camera will photograph the entire visible southern sky every few nights for ten years, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time. For the ladder this means supernovae by the million, rather than the thousands found so far, and with them a far better test of how the brightness of Type Ia explosions depends on their host galaxies. The first-look images were released on 23 June 2025, and the full survey began in mid 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It will multiply the supernovae at the top of the ladder by orders of magnitude.
spotlights.memory_hook: A camera that films the whole southern sky every few nights.

spotlights.name: Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope
spotlights.spot_it: A Hubble-sized 2.4 metre mirror with a field of view about 100 times wider than Hubble's cameras.
spotlights.story_md: Roman is named after NASA's first chief astronomer, who championed the Hubble Space Telescope. Its 2.4 metre mirror was donated by the National Reconnaissance Office. It survived proposed budget cuts in 2025, was finished in November 2025, and launched on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center on 30 August 2026. Among its main jobs is a supernova survey to measure the expansion history, plus galaxy maps and gravitational lensing, three independent probes of dark energy from one telescope.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It will add thousands of distant supernovae measured with Hubble-like sharpness.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hubble's eyesight, a hundred times the view.

spotlights.name: Andromeda collision: a coin toss
spotlights.spot_it: A forecast, not a picture: our galaxy and its neighbour may or may not merge in the next 10 billion years.
spotlights.story_md: Textbooks long said the Milky Way and Andromeda will collide in about 4.5 billion years. Till Sawala and colleagues reran the forecast in 2025 using Gaia and Hubble measurements of both galaxies' motions, plus the pull of nearby galaxies such as Triangulum and the Large Magellanic Cloud. They ran 100,000 simulations across the range allowed by the measurement uncertainties. About half ended in a merger within 10 billion years; in the other half the galaxies passed without merging in that time.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Precise distances change not just numbers but the stories we tell about the future.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Milky Way's fate became a coin flip.

sections.title: Recap: how we know
sections.intro_md:
Start with the Earth. A shadow in Alexandria gave its size; lasers off Apollo and Chandrayaan reflectors now give the Moon's distance to a millimetre. Kepler's laws gave the solar system's shape, transits of Venus and then radar gave its size, and in 2012 the astronomical unit became an exact definition.

With the Earth's orbit as a baseline, parallax gives distances to nearby stars: Bessel's 61 Cygni in 1838, Hipparcos' 118,000 stars, Gaia's billion. Parallax calibrates Cepheids, whose period reveals their power, thanks to Leavitt's 1912 graph. Cepheids carried Hubble to Andromeda in 1923 and to the expansion law in 1929. Baade doubled the scale in 1952. Geometric anchors such as eclipsing binaries and masers, and new candles like red giants, now cross-check the Cepheids. Cepheids and red giants calibrate Type Ia supernovae, which reach billions of light years and showed the expansion is accelerating.

Ladder-free methods, from the CMB to gravitational wave sirens, mostly land near 67 to 70. The ladder lands near 73. Either one rung hides a few percent of error, or the universe is doing something our model leaves out. Both answers would be worth knowing.

cards.front: What did Henrietta Leavitt find in 1912?
cards.back: Cepheid variables with longer pulsation periods are intrinsically brighter: the period-luminosity law.

cards.front: Who is this Harvard astronomer, paid 30 cents an hour?
cards.back: Henrietta Swan Leavitt.

cards.front: Leavitt's 1912 paper timed ___ Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud.
Why did it matter that Leavitt's stars were all in the Small Magellanic Cloud?
cards.back: They were all at about the same distance, so differences in apparent brightness were differences in true brightness.

cards.front: What was this group of women at Harvard College Observatory called?
cards.back: The Harvard computers, who read and measured glass photographic plates.

cards.front: What is the cosmic distance ladder?
cards.back: A chain of distance methods where each rung calibrates the next, from geometry close by to standard candles and redshift far away.

cards.front: How long is one parsec?
cards.back: About 3.26 light years: the distance at which 1 AU subtends one arcsecond.

cards.front: Since 2012 the astronomical unit is defined as exactly ___ metres.
How did Eratosthenes measure the Earth?
cards.back: A noon shadow angle of about 7.2 degrees in Alexandria, when the Sun was overhead at Syene, times the distance between them: about 250,000 stadia.

cards.front: Aristarchus' method for the Sun's distance was sound. Why was his answer 20 times too small?
cards.back: He measured the Moon-Earth-Sun angle as 87 degrees; the true value is about 89.85. Tiny angles cause huge errors.

cards.front: What did Hipparchus use to estimate the Moon's distance?
cards.back: A solar eclipse seen as total in one place and partial in another: the Moon's parallax.

cards.front: Why were transits of Venus so valuable?
cards.back: Timing Venus crossing the Sun from far-apart places gave its parallax and so the Sun's distance, the scale of the whole solar system.

cards.front: What event is shown here, last seen in 2012 and next due in 2117?
cards.back: A transit of Venus across the Sun.

cards.front: What spoiled transit timings in the 18th century?
cards.back: The black drop effect: Venus seemed to stick to the Sun's edge.

cards.front: Which astronomer missed both 1761 and 1769 transits, the second at Pondicherry, and came home to find himself declared dead?
cards.back: Guillaume Le Gentil.

cards.front: How did radar in 1961 change the measurement of the AU?
cards.back: Timing radio echoes off Venus gave its distance directly, fixing the AU far better than centuries of optical work.

cards.front: What is this object on the Moon and what does it do?
cards.back: Apollo 11's laser ranging retroreflector; it returns laser pulses so Earth-Moon distance can be timed to about a millimetre.

cards.front: Lunar laser ranging shows the Moon receding by about ___ cm a year.
Who published the first reliable stellar parallax, for which star, and when?
cards.back: Friedrich Bessel, 61 Cygni, 1838.

cards.front: Who is this Königsberg astronomer?
cards.back: Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel.

cards.front: Why did Bessel pick 61 Cygni rather than a bright star?
cards.back: It had a very large motion across the sky, suggesting it was close.

cards.front: Which star system did Thomas Henderson measure, and why did he lose priority?
cards.back: Alpha Centauri; he delayed reducing and publishing his Cape data until after Bessel.

cards.front: Which satellite is this: Hipparcos (1989) or Gaia (2013)?
cards.back: Gaia, with its round sunshield.

cards.front: When did Gaia stop observing, and when is Data Release 4 scheduled?
cards.back: Science observations ended 15 January 2025; switched off 27 March 2025; DR4 scheduled for 2 December 2026.

cards.front: What was wrong with Hipparcos' Pleiades distance?
cards.back: About 120 pc instead of about 136 pc; a radio parallax in 2014 and Gaia confirmed the larger value.

cards.front: What is a standard candle?
cards.back: An object whose true brightness is known, so its apparent brightness gives its distance through the inverse square law.

cards.front: What makes Cepheids pulse?
cards.back: The Eddington valve: helium ionisation in the outer layers traps and releases heat, so the star swells and shrinks.

cards.front: Who found that Delta Cephei varies?
cards.back: John Goodricke, a deaf young astronomer in York, in 1784.

cards.front: This famous Hubble image shows rings of light rippling through dust around a pulsing star. Name the star.
cards.back: RS Puppis, whose light echo gave a geometric distance of about 6,500 light years.

cards.front: Why does Polaris matter for the ladder, and why is it awkward?
cards.back: It is the nearest Cepheid, yet its distance estimates have ranged from about 323 to about 446 light years.

cards.front: What was the 1920 Great Debate about?
cards.back: Whether spiral nebulae were inside the Milky Way (Shapley) or separate galaxies (Curtis).

cards.front: This astronomer marked a star on a 1923 plate of Andromeda 'N', then crossed it out. Who was he, and what did he write instead?
cards.back: Edwin Hubble; he wrote VAR!, because the 'nova' was a Cepheid variable.

cards.front: Name this galaxy, the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye.
cards.back: The Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light years away.

cards.front: Which telescope did Hubble use to find Cepheids in Andromeda?
cards.back: The Hooker 100-inch telescope on Mount Wilson, largest in the world 1917 to 1949.

cards.front: What does the Hubble constant measure, and in what units?
cards.back: How fast galaxies recede per unit distance: km per second per megaparsec.

cards.front: Hubble's 1929 value of H0 was about ___ km/s per Mpc, roughly seven times today's.
Who is this Belgian priest who described the expanding universe in 1927?
cards.back: Georges Lemaître.

cards.front: What did Walter Baade announce in Rome in 1952?
cards.back: There are two kinds of Cepheid; correcting for it roughly doubled the extragalactic distance scale.

cards.front: Who measured spiral nebula velocities from 1912 at Lowell Observatory?
cards.back: Vesto Slipher.

cards.front: How did the 2019 eclipsing binary study measure the Large Magellanic Cloud?
cards.back: 20 eclipsing pairs of giant stars gave physical and angular sizes: 49.59 kpc to about 1%.

cards.front: How do water masers in NGC 4258 give a distance?
cards.back: Their orbital speeds and drifts across the sky give the disc's true and angular size: 7.58 Mpc, pure geometry.

cards.front: Why is the tip of the red giant branch a standard candle?
cards.back: Red giants ignite helium at almost the same core mass, so the brightest ones peak at nearly the same luminosity.

cards.front: What makes Type Ia supernovae nearly standard?
cards.back: They are white dwarfs blowing up near the Chandrasekhar mass, about 1.4 Suns; the Phillips relation corrects the rest.

cards.front: The bright new star in this galaxy was found by a class in London in 2014. What kind of explosion was it?
cards.back: A Type Ia supernova, SN 2014J, in M82.

cards.front: What did the 1998 and 1999 supernova results show, and who won the Nobel for it?
cards.back: The expansion is accelerating; Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess, 2011.

cards.front: What is a standard siren?
cards.back: A gravitational wave source whose signal gives its distance directly, like the neutron star merger GW170817.

cards.front: What does this oval map show, and what H0 does it imply?
cards.back: The cosmic microwave background from Planck; with the standard model, H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5.

cards.front: State the Hubble tension in two numbers.
cards.back: Distance ladder about 73; early-universe prediction about 67.4 km/s per Mpc.

cards.front: What H0 did Freedman's CCHP report in 2025 using JWST red giants?
cards.back: 70.39, with a total uncertainty of about 2.

cards.front: What is the Pogson ratio and why does it matter for distances?
cards.back: Each magnitude step is the fifth root of 100, about 2.512; it underlies the distance modulus.

cards.front: Who is this physicist from Madras whose mass limit makes Type Ia supernovae uniform?
cards.back: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.

cards.front: What did Chandrayaan-3 carry that adds to lunar laser ranging?
cards.back: NASA's Laser Retroreflector Array on the Vikram lander, pinged from lunar orbit on 12 December 2023.

cards.front: Where is LIGO-India being built?
cards.back: Near Aundha Nagnath, Hingoli district, Maharashtra.

cards.front: What did Aryabhata say about the Earth in 499 CE?
cards.back: That it rotates on its axis, and the stars' daily motion is an effect of that rotation.

cards.front: What did the IAU recommend in 2018 about Hubble's law?
cards.back: Calling it the Hubble-Lemaître law; 78% of voting members agreed.

cards.front: What did the H0 Distance Network report in April 2026?
cards.back: A consensus local value of 73.50 ± 0.81 km/s per Mpc.

cards.front: Why does a sailor's distance by dead reckoning resemble the distance ladder?
cards.back: Each estimate builds on the one before, so small errors compound unless checked against an independent fix.

cards.front: What independent fix did 18th-century navigators gain from astronomy?
cards.back: Longitude by lunar distances and the marine chronometer, which reset accumulated dead-reckoning error.
