best_facts.fact: Henrietta Leavitt, who found the rule used to measure galaxies, was paid 30 cents an hour and was nominated for a Nobel Prize three years after she died.
best_facts.why_surprising: The key to the universe's size came from a low-paid assistant.

best_facts.fact: The first star distance ever measured, 61 Cygni in 1838, needed an angle of about 0.3 arcseconds: roughly the width of a small coin seen from 7 km.
best_facts.why_surprising: It took 2,000 years of searching because the angle was that small.

best_facts.fact: Hubble proved Andromeda is a separate galaxy with one photographic plate on which he crossed out 'N' and wrote 'VAR!'.
best_facts.why_surprising: A single scribbled word changed the universe from one galaxy to billions.

best_facts.fact: Wartime blackouts in Los Angeles let Walter Baade see individual stars in Andromeda's core, which led to the discovery that the universe was twice as big as thought.
best_facts.why_surprising: A war doubled the size of the universe.

best_facts.fact: Guillaume Le Gentil spent 11 years chasing two transits of Venus, saw neither, and came home to find he had been declared dead and his estate divided.
best_facts.why_surprising: Science's unluckiest trip was over one number.

best_facts.fact: The two best ways of measuring the universe's expansion disagree: about 73 from the distance ladder and about 67.4 from the early universe, with both claiming about 1% precision.
best_facts.why_surprising: Our most precise science cannot agree on one basic number.

best_facts.fact: Hubble's 1929 expansion rate implied the universe was about 2 billion years old, younger than rocks on Earth.
best_facts.why_surprising: The founding measurement of modern cosmology was badly wrong.

best_facts.fact: Of the hundreds of quadrillions of photons fired at an Apollo reflector in each attempt, only a handful come back, yet they measure the Moon's distance to about a millimetre.
Since 2012 the distance from Earth to the Sun has not been measured at all. It is defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.
best_facts.why_surprising: After 2,000 years of measuring, astronomers simply fixed it.

best_facts.fact: The Cepheid story begins and peaks with deaf astronomers: John Goodricke found Delta Cephei's variability in 1784, and Henrietta Leavitt found the law that uses it.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two deaf observers bracket one of astronomy's key tools.

best_facts.fact: Georges Lemaître published the expanding universe and an expansion rate two years before Hubble, then cut his own number from the English translation.
In 2017 two neutron stars colliding 130 million years ago gave a measurement of the universe's expansion with no distance ladder at all.
best_facts.why_surprising: Gravitational waves are a ruler built into spacetime.

best_facts.fact: Chandrasekhar worked out the white dwarf mass limit at 19, on a ship from Madras to England; that limit is why exploding white dwarfs work as standard candles.
best_facts.why_surprising: A shipboard calculation underpins the discovery of dark energy.

best_facts.fact: The nearest Type Ia supernova in 42 years, SN 2014J, was found by a lecturer and four students during a teaching session in north London.
best_facts.why_surprising: A class beat the world's survey telescopes.

best_facts.fact: The Hooker telescope that found other galaxies had a mirror cast from French wine-bottle glass, full of bubbles.
best_facts.why_surprising: Cosmology's biggest leap rested on recycled glass.

best_facts.fact: Even the North Star's distance has been disputed by about 30%, from about 323 to about 446 light years, though it is the nearest Cepheid.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous star has an uncertain address.

best_facts.fact: Better distances and motions turned the 'certain' Milky Way-Andromeda collision into roughly a 50-50 chance within 10 billion years (2025).
best_facts.why_surprising: Precision made the future less certain, not more.

best_facts.fact: Pogson discovered an asteroid from Madras in 1861 and named it 67 Asia, the first asteroid found from the continent.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's link to the ladder runs through a Chennai observatory.

side_dish.title: Dead reckoning: the sailor's distance ladder
side_dish.body_md:
Before satellites, a ship's navigator worked out position by **dead reckoning**: start from a known point, then add speed multiplied by time along the compass heading. Speed came from a log line, a knotted rope paid out behind the ship and timed with a sandglass, which is why ship speeds are still measured in knots.

Each new position was built on the last one, exactly like a rung on the distance ladder. That made the method fragile. A small error in speed, a current nobody had noticed, or a compass a degree off would compound, hour after hour, and after weeks at sea the ship could be tens of kilometres from where the chart said. Wrecks were often blamed on accumulated dead-reckoning errors.

The cure was the same one astronomers use: an independent fix that does not depend on the chain. For latitude, sailors measured the Sun at noon. For longitude, the 18th century produced two rival fixes: John Harrison's marine chronometer and the lunar distance method, which timed the Moon against stars using tables built by astronomers. Cook carried both on his second voyage.

The lesson carries straight back to today's topic. When the Hubble tension appeared, astronomers did what navigators did: they looked for fixes that skip the chain, such as gravitational wave sirens and lensing delays. If those land on the ladder's number, the chain is sound. If they land elsewhere, someone has a current they have not noticed.

offline_task.title: Measure a distance with your thumb
offline_task.body_md:
You will use parallax, the first stellar rung, on something across a room or a street.

1. Stand facing a distant object, such as a lamp post or a window frame, with a wall or skyline behind it.
2. Hold your thumb up at arm's length. Close your left eye and line your thumb up with the object. Now switch eyes. Your thumb jumps sideways.
3. Estimate how far it jumped, measured at the distant object, in metres: for example, 'about two car widths'.
4. Your arm is roughly 10 times longer than the distance between your eyes. So the object is roughly 10 times farther away than the size of the jump.
5. Check by pacing the distance if you can.

This is exactly what Bessel did with 61 Cygni, except his 'eyes' were Earth's positions six months apart, 300 million km apart, and his jump was a third of an arcsecond. Tonight, if it is clear, find the North Star or, from a dark site in autumn, the faint smudge of the Andromeda Galaxy, and remember that each has a distance someone fought to measure.
